title: Is the diagonal of a rectangle a line of symmetry?
description: A rectangle that is longer than it is wide is folded corner to corner. The two parts are compared to see whether they overlap. Keeko doubts that it differs from a square.
teaching_notes: One idea: a diagonal is a line of symmetry only when the two parts overlap exactly, which is true for a square but not for a rectangle that is not a square. Watch for students who carry the square's result over to the rectangle.

source: We saw that the diagonal of a square is also a line of symmetry. Take a rectangle that is not a square. Is its diagonal a line of symmetry? First see the rectangle and answer, then take a rectangular piece of paper and check by folding along its diagonal whether the two parts overlap.
video_script.why: The child tests whether a result for the square carries over to a rectangle, and finds that it does not.
video_script.substitution: Fold a rectangular piece of paper corner to corner and see whether the two parts overlap.
video_script.anchor: A rectangle that is longer than it is wide, folded corner to corner
video_script.wrong_answer: the diagonal of a rectangle is a line of symmetry
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the diagonal of a rectangle is a line of symmetry because the diagonal of a square is. Folding the rectangle shows the long side landing on the short side, so the idea is struck out.
video_script.payoff_line: A diagonal is a line of symmetry only if the parts overlap.

final_answer.value: No; the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square is not a line of symmetry
final_answer.spoken: no, the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square is not a line of symmetry

never_show: the verdict before the answer beat
maths_rules: A line of symmetry is a fold line along which one half covers the other exactly.
A diagonal is a line joining two opposite corners.
Folding a rectangle that is longer than it is wide along its diagonal: the two corners off the diagonal do not meet, and the long side lands on the short side.
A long side cannot cover a short side, so the two parts do not overlap.
The matching folds of a rectangle are straight down and straight across, not the diagonals.
video_script.design: One idea: a diagonal is a line of symmetry only if the parts overlap exactly. Assumes the child knows the square has diagonal folds that match. The rectangle stays on the board from the hook to the end.
